title: Dinner at a restaurant
goal: Order a full meal from starter to dessert, ask about the menu, and pay.
bekal: ordering the three courses of a French meal in the right words
using *je prends* and *pour moi* when ordering
giving an opinion about food: *c'est délicieux*
wave: Review **Unit 11** first: describe three people you know — height, hair, personality — and compare them with each other.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Le menu du soir
dialogs.intro: Budi and Camille are having dinner at a small bistro.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Oui. Je prends le menu à vingt-deux euros.
lines.id: Yes. I'll have the twenty-two-euro set menu.
lines.literal: yes. I take the menu at twenty-two euros.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Une soupe à l'oignon, s'il vous plaît.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Le poulet rôti avec des frites.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Pour moi, une salade de chèvre chaud, puis du poisson.
lines.id: For me, a warm goat cheese salad, then the fish.
lines.literal: for me, a salad of goat hot, then some fish.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Une carafe d'eau, s'il vous plaît. C'est gratuit, non ?
lines.id: A jug of tap water, please. It's free, isn't it?
lines.literal: a jug of-water, please. it-is free, no?

lines.speaker: Serveuse:
lines.text: Bien sûr. Je vous apporte ça tout de suite.
lines.id: Of course. I'll bring it right away.
lines.literal: well sure. I to-you it bring all of following.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Merci. Et l'addition à la fin, s'il vous plaît.
lines.id: Thank you. And the check at the end, please.
lines.literal: thanks. and the bill at-the end, please.

notes: **A French dinner has three acts.** *L'entrée* (starter), *le plat principal* (main course), *le dessert*. ⚠️ *Entrée* means the starter, **not** the main course as in American English — a trap that catches many tourists.
**Le menu is not the list of dishes.** The list of dishes is *la carte*. *Le menu* means a fixed-price set meal. That's why ordering "à la carte" means choosing dishes one by one, outside the set.
**Une carafe d'eau is free, and it's your right.** French restaurants must serve free tap water if you ask. If you just say *de l'eau*, you may be handed paid bottled water.
**Pour moi** is the easiest way to give your own order when the server moves around the table. Its cousins are *je prends…* and *je vais prendre…* All three are used interchangeably.
**Comme entrée, comme boisson** — *comme* here means "as", not "like". Servers all over France use this pattern.
**Tout de suite** (too duh SWEET) = right away, right now. One of the time phrases you'll hear most in restaurants and shops.
**Bien sûr** = of course. Don't confuse it with plain *bien* (well). Its relaxed cousins are *évidemment* and *bien entendu*.

grammars.title: Verbs for ordering
body: Four verbs that cover a whole restaurant conversation. You already know two of them.
after: ⚠️ *Je veux* sounds rude in a restaurant — like a child making demands. Adults say *je voudrais* (the polite form) or *je prends*.
*Vouloir* expresses a strong wish, and its polite form is the only *conditionnel* you need to master at A1: *je voudrais, tu voudrais, il voudrait, nous voudrions, vous voudriez, ils voudraient*.

grammars.title: Giving an opinion about food
body: The adjectives you'll hear most at a French table, from the warmest praise to the clearest rejection.
after: ⚠️ *Bon* is for taste, *bien* is for how something is done. The food is *bon*, but the chef cooks *bien* — like "good" versus "well". Mixing them up is one of the most common mistakes foreign learners make.
*Ce n'est pas mal* sounds weak, but to French ears it's fairly warm praise.

blocks.title: Lifesaving phrases
items: *Une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît.* — A table for two, please.
*Qu'est-ce que vous me conseillez ?* — What do you recommend?
*Je suis allergique aux fruits de mer.* — I'm allergic to seafood.
*L'addition, s'il vous plaît.* — The check, please.
*On peut payer séparément ?* — Can we pay separately?
